title: Tokens and the Next Word
objective: After this level you can explain how a large language model splits text into tokens and writes by predicting one token after another.
summary: Text is chopped into subword tokens, each swapped for a number. The model scores every token in its vocabulary, one is picked and appended, and the loop repeats.

cards.headline: A chatbot may never see the word "annoyingly" whole.
cards.body: Before a language model reads your message, the text is chopped into pieces, and every piece is swapped for a number. You met tokens in Everyday Technology. Here's what actually happens to your words on the way in, and how a reply comes out.

cards.headline: Chopping text into tokens
cards.body: Most language models use subword tokens. Frequent words stay whole, while rare words are split into meaningful pieces that turn up more often: "annoyingly" becomes "annoying" plus "ly". That way a fixed list of pieces can still cover words the model rarely met, and the meaning survives in the parts.

cards.headline: Every token gets a number
cards.body: Models can only process numbers, so the tokenizer swaps each token for its ID: its number in the model's vocabulary. GPT-2, from 2019, had a vocabulary of 50,257 tokens. It's Level 4's idea one size up. Unicode gives a number to every character; a tokenizer gives a number to every chunk.

cards.headline: One token, then again
cards.body: To write, the model gives a score to every token in its vocabulary, and one is picked. That token is added to the text, and the whole thing goes back in for the next pick, so each new token depends on all the ones before it. A setting called temperature shapes the pick: higher is more random, lower more focused and predictable.

mascot.line: Keep this: a chatbot never picks a whole answer. It picks one token, then starts again with that token added.
